claim: Spiroplasma poulsonii is a maternally transmitted bacterial endosymbiont that is naturally associated with Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Spiroplasma poulsonii is a maternally transmitted bacterial endosymbiont that is naturally associated with Drosophila melanogaster.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the Spiroplasma-Drosophila association.

claim: S. poulsonii resides extracellularly in the hemolymph.
source: S. poulsonii resides extracellularly in the hemolymph, where it must acquire metabolites to sustain proliferation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Spiroplasma's localization in the host.

claim: Spiroplasma proliferation specifically depletes host hemolymph diacylglyceride.
source: In this study, we find that Spiroplasma proliferation specifically depletes host hemolymph diacylglyceride, the major lipid class transported by the lipoprotein, Lpp.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing DAG depletion in Spiroplasma-infected flies.

claim: Diacylglyceride is the major lipid class transported by the lipoprotein, Lpp.
source: In this study, we find that Spiroplasma proliferation specifically depletes host hemolymph diacylglyceride, the major lipid class transported by the lipoprotein, Lpp.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila lipid transport.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Lpp expression reduces the amount of circulating lipids.
source: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Lpp expression, which reduces the amount of circulating lipids, inhibits Spiroplasma proliferation demonstrating that bacterial proliferation requires hemolymph-lipids.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced hemolymph lipids upon Lpp knockdown.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Lpp expression inhibits Spiroplasma proliferation.
source: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Lpp expression, which reduces the amount of circulating lipids, inhibits Spiroplasma proliferation demonstrating that bacterial proliferation requires hemolymph-lipids.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced Spiroplasma titers upon Lpp knockdown.

claim: Bacterial proliferation requires hemolymph-lipids.
source: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Lpp expression, which reduces the amount of circulating lipids, inhibits Spiroplasma proliferation demonstrating that bacterial proliferation requires hemolymph-lipids.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that reducing hemolymph lipids inhibits Spiroplasma proliferation.

claim: An insect endosymbiont acquires specific lipidic metabolites from the transport lipoproteins in the hemolymph of its host.
source: Altogether, our study shows that an insect endosymbiont acquires specific lipidic metabolites from the transport lipoproteins in the hemolymph of its host.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing DAG depletion and cardiolipin production by Spiroplasma.

claim: The proliferation of this endosymbiont is limited by the availability of hemolymph lipids.
source: In addition, we show that the proliferation of this endosymbiont is limited by the availability of hemolymph lipids.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced Spiroplasma proliferation under nutrient limitation and Lpp knockdown.

claim: Lipid availability is strongly influenced by the nutritional state.
source: This feature could limit endosymbiont over-proliferation under conditions of host nutrient limitation as lipid availability is strongly influenced by the nutritional state.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced hemolymph lipids under nutrient limitation.

claim: Wolbachia and Spiroplasma are estimated to infect ∼40% and 5–10% of all insects species, respectively.
source: Two of the most prevalent and well-characterized facultative insect endosymbionts are Wolbachia and Spiroplasma, which are estimated to infect ∼40% and 5–10% of all insects species, respectively (Hackett and Clark, 1979; Duron et al., 2008; Hilgenboecker et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Wolbachia principally resides intracellularly.
source: While Wolbachia principally resides intracellularly (Dobson et al., 1999; Albertson et al., 2009), Spiroplasma occupies an extracellular niche, proliferating mainly in the hemolymph that fills the body cavity of arthropods (Sakaguchi and Poulson, 1961; Anbutsu and Fukatsu, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Spiroplasma occupies an extracellular niche, proliferating mainly in the hemolymph that fills the body cavity of arthropods.
source: While Wolbachia principally resides intracellularly (Dobson et al., 1999; Albertson et al., 2009), Spiroplasma occupies an extracellular niche, proliferating mainly in the hemolymph that fills the body cavity of arthropods (Sakaguchi and Poulson, 1961; Anbutsu and Fukatsu, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Spiroplasma and Wolbachia are both maternally transmitted.
source: Spiroplasma and Wolbachia are both maternally transmitted and have developed unique strategies to colonize the germline of their female hosts for transmission to the next generation (Frydman et al., 2006; Serbus and Sullivan, 2007; Herren et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Spiroplasma and Wolbachia have developed unique strategies to colonize the germline of their female hosts for transmission to the next generation.
source: Spiroplasma and Wolbachia are both maternally transmitted and have developed unique strategies to colonize the germline of their female hosts for transmission to the next generation (Frydman et al., 2006; Serbus and Sullivan, 2007; Herren et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Genome sequencing has indicated that endosymbiotic bacteria have highly reduced metabolic capacities and depend heavily on their hosts to provide them with a diversity of compounds needed for their sustained proliferation.
source: Genome sequencing has indicated that endosymbiotic bacteria have highly reduced metabolic capacities and depend heavily on their hosts to provide them with a diversity of compounds needed for their sustained proliferation (Klein et al., 2012; Moran et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genomic studies.

claim: Flies-harboring Spiroplasma have a significantly shortened life span compared to flies that do not harbor Spiroplasma when maintained on a rich Drosophila diet.
source: When maintained on a rich Drosophila diet, flies-harboring Spiroplasma have a significantly shortened life span compared to flies that do not harbor Spiroplasma (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), which is in agreement with a previous study on Drosophila willistoni and WSRO Spiroplasma (Ebbert, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by experimental survival data shown in Figure 1A and cited previous studies.

claim: The presence of Spiroplasma did not significantly affect the death rate until flies were about 21–25 days old.
source: Notably, the presence of Spiroplasma did not significantly affect the death rate until flies were about 21–25 days old but flies began to exhibit signs of Spiroplasma-induced pathology between 14 and 21 days, as demonstrated by decreased performance in climbing assays (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1B.

claim: Flies began to exhibit signs of Spiroplasma-induced pathology between 14 and 21 days, as demonstrated by decreased performance in climbing assays.
source: Notably, the presence of Spiroplasma did not significantly affect the death rate until flies were about 21–25 days old but flies began to exhibit signs of Spiroplasma-induced pathology between 14 and 21 days, as demonstrated by decreased performance in climbing assays (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The increase in Spiroplasma-induced lethality and pathology in old flies correlates with the increase of Spiroplasma titers.
source: The increase in Spiroplasma-induced lethality and pathology in old flies correlates with the increase of Spiroplasma titers, observed by qPCR of whole flies (Figure 1C) and fluorescence microscopy of hemolymph (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: Spiroplasma titers reached a plateau in old flies (age >28 days).
source: Consistent with previous studies on other Drosophila-endosymbiotic Spiroplasma strains (Anbutsu and Fukatsu, 2003; Haselkorn et al., 2013), we noticed that Spiroplasma titers reached a plateau in old flies (age >28 days) suggesting that a factor might limit Spiroplasma proliferation at this stage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: There was a twofold increase in the number of eggs laid by Spiroplasma-infected virgin flies compared to Spiroplasma-uninfected virgin flies over 14 days.
source: There was a twofold increase in the number of eggs laid by Spiroplasma-infected virgin flies compared to Spiroplasma-uninfected virgin flies over 14 days (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Spiroplasma-infected mated flies laid an increased number of eggs in the first 2 days post-eclosion.
source: The number of eggs laid by Spiroplasma-infected mated flies over a 14-day period was similar to Spiroplasma-uninfected mated flies, however, Spiroplasma-infected mated flies laid an increased number of eggs in the first 2 days post-eclosion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Spiroplasma-infected and uninfected virgin flies had a similar life span under nutrient-limiting conditions.
source: Surprisingly, Spiroplasma-infected and uninfected virgin flies had a similar life span (Figure 2A) and produced similar numbers of eggs under nutrient-limiting conditions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Spiroplasma-infected and uninfected virgin flies produced similar numbers of eggs under nutrient-limiting conditions.
source: Surprisingly, Spiroplasma-infected and uninfected virgin flies had a similar life span (Figure 2A) and produced similar numbers of eggs under nutrient-limiting conditions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Spiroplasma proliferation in whole flies was significantly inhibited when flies are maintained on a nutrient poor diet.
source: Importantly, we observed that Spiroplasma proliferation in whole flies (Figure 2B) and hemolymph (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) was also significantly inhibited when flies are maintained on a nutrient poor diet.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Raising flies on a nutrient poor diet resulted in significantly lower concentrations of protein, sterol and diacylglyceride in the hemolymph.
source: We found that raising flies on a nutrient poor diet resulted in significantly lower concentrations of protein, sterol and diacylglyceride (DAG, the main transport lipid in Drosophila) (Figure 3A–C), while levels of glucose and trehalose were not changed significantly (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B) and L-amino acids increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A-C.

claim: Levels of glucose and trehalose were not changed significantly under nutrient limitation.
source: We found that raising flies on a nutrient poor diet resulted in significantly lower concentrations of protein, sterol and diacylglyceride (DAG, the main transport lipid in Drosophila) (Figure 3A–C), while levels of glucose and trehalose were not changed significantly (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B) and L-amino acids increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: L-amino acids increased under nutrient limitation.
source: We found that raising flies on a nutrient poor diet resulted in significantly lower concentrations of protein, sterol and diacylglyceride (DAG, the main transport lipid in Drosophila) (Figure 3A–C), while levels of glucose and trehalose were not changed significantly (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B) and L-amino acids increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Only inactivated yeast extract was able to recover the Spiroplasma proliferation rates observed on rich media.
source: We then complemented the nutrient poor diet with either inactivated yeast (rich in protein and lipids) or sucrose, we found that only inactivated yeast extract was able to recover the Spiroplasma proliferation rates observed on rich media (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The concentration of measured sugars was not changed in the hemolymph of flies-harboring Spiroplasma raised on a rich diet.
source: We observed that the concentration of measured sugars was not changed and that the L-amino acid concentration was even increased in the presence of Spiroplasma (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5A-B.

claim: The L-amino acid concentration was increased in the presence of Spiroplasma.
source: We observed that the concentration of measured sugars was not changed and that the L-amino acid concentration was even increased in the presence of Spiroplasma (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The hemolymph of flies-harboring Spiroplasma had an increased concentration of proteins and sterol.
source: We also found that the hemolymph of flies-harboring Spiroplasma had an increased concentration of proteins and sterol (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: After centrifugation to remove bacterial cells, the protein and sterol concentration was no longer significantly different between Spiroplasma-infected and Spiroplasma-uninfected hemolymph samples.
source: However, after centrifugation to remove bacterial cells, the protein and sterol concentration was no longer significantly different between Spiroplasma-infected and Spiroplasma-uninfected hemolymph samples.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: Spiroplasma cells contain a substantial amount of proteins and sterol.
source: This suggests that Spiroplasma cells contain a substantial amount of proteins and sterol, but that the presence of this endosymbiont does not deplete either of these factors in the hemolymph.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that protein and sterol levels are higher in total hemolymph but not in supernatant after removing Spiroplasma cells.

claim: The presence of Spiroplasma does not deplete protein or sterol in the hemolymph.
source: This suggests that Spiroplasma cells contain a substantial amount of proteins and sterol, but that the presence of this endosymbiont does not deplete either of these factors in the hemolymph.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data showing no difference in supernatant protein and sterol levels.

claim: Spiroplasma-infected flies experienced a significant drop in the concentration of DAG within the hemolymph.
source: Notably, we observed that Spiroplasma-infected flies experienced a significant drop in the concentration of DAG within the hemolymph (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: There was a decrease in the amount of TAG in Spiroplasma-infected flies compared to Spiroplasma-uninfected flies.
source: Quantifications of whole female flies (reflecting mainly insect fat body energy storage but also the energy contents of the ovaries) showed a decrease in the amount of TAG in Spiroplasma-infected flies compared to Spiroplasma-uninfected flies (Figure 5G), while the amount of glycogen was not affected by the presence of Spiroplasma (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The amount of glycogen was not affected by the presence of Spiroplasma.
source: Quantifications of whole female flies (reflecting mainly insect fat body energy storage but also the energy contents of the ovaries) showed a decrease in the amount of TAG in Spiroplasma-infected flies compared to Spiroplasma-uninfected flies (Figure 5G), while the amount of glycogen was not affected by the presence of Spiroplasma (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: 12-day-old Spiroplasma-infected flies succumb more rapidly to acute starvation.
source: Consistent with the decrease in TAG reserves, 12-day-old Spiroplasma-infected flies succumb more rapidly to acute starvation, in which flies are only given a source of water but no source of nutrition (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: TAG stored in the fat body largely derived from hemolymph DAG.
source: Since TAG stored in the fat body largely derived from hemolymph DAG (Canavoso et al., 2001), the decrease of TAG is likely to be the outcome of the depletion of hemolymphatic DAG by Spiroplasma.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: The decrease of TAG is likely to be the outcome of the depletion of hemolymphatic DAG by Spiroplasma.
source: Since TAG stored in the fat body largely derived from hemolymph DAG (Canavoso et al., 2001), the decrease of TAG is likely to be the outcome of the depletion of hemolymphatic DAG by Spiroplasma.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both hemolymph DAG and fat body TAG are depleted in Spiroplasma-infected flies.

claim: The main classes of lipids that are present in Spiroplasma are phosphatidylglycerols, sterols, sphingolipids, and cardiolipins.
source: The main classes of lipids that are present in Spiroplasma are phosphatidylglycerols, sterols, sphingolipids, and cardiolipins (Freeman et al., 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: Cardiolipins are a class of lipids found exclusively in eubacteria and in the mitochondria of eukaryotic cells.
source: Cardiolipins are a class of lipids found exclusively in eubacteria and in the mitochondria of eukaryotic cells (Hawthorne and Ansell, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: Cardiolipins are not present at detectable levels in the Drosophila hemolymph.
source: In contrast to other major lipidic components of Spiroplasma membranes, cardiolipins are not present at detectable levels in the Drosophila hemolymph (Carvalho et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: There were only peaks at m/z values that correspond to cardiolipin in the hemolymph of flies-harboring Spiroplasma.
source: To investigate the production of cardiolipin by Spiroplasma, we conducted a MALDI time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-Tof-MS) analysis of lipid species in fly hemolymph and found that there were only peaks at m/z values that correspond to cardiolipin in the hemolymph of flies-harboring Spiroplasma (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The cardiolipins were comprised of C16:0 and C18:1 acyl chains.
source: A major ion at m/z 1425.05 was isolated and fragmented, which confirmed the presence of cardiolipin and revealed that the cardiolipins were comprised of C16:0 and C18:1 acyl chains (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Overall DAG concentration declined by 16.3% in the presence of Spiroplasma.
source: We observed that overall DAG concentration declined by 16.3%, however certain DAG species (e.g., C32:1 and C34:1 DAG) declined to a much greater extent (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental LC-MS/MS data shown in Table 1.

claim: Certain DAG species (e.g., C32:1 and C34:1 DAG) declined to a much greater extent than overall DAG.
source: We observed that overall DAG concentration declined by 16.3%, however certain DAG species (e.g., C32:1 and C34:1 DAG) declined to a much greater extent (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental LC-MS/MS data shown in Table 1.

claim: Spiroplasma most likely produce cardiolipin using fly hemolymph DAG.
source: The observation that Spiroplasma-generated cardiolipin contains the same configuration of one saturated and one mono-unsaturated medium-length acyl chain (predominately C16:0, C18:1) indicates that Spiroplasma most likely produce cardiolipin using fly hemolymph DAG.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cardiolipin acyl chains match those of depleted DAG species.

claim: The transformation of DAG into cardiolipin offers an explanation for the observed decrease in hemolymph DAG levels in the presence of Spiroplasma.
source: The transformation of DAG into cardiolipin offers an explanation for the observed decrease in hemolymph DAG levels in the presence of Spiroplasma.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that DAG is depleted and cardiolipin is produced in Spiroplasma-infected flies.

claim: Lpp is produced in the fat body but travels to the gut where it gets loaded with lipids prior to trafficking throughout the body.
source: Lpp is produced in the fat body but travels to the gut where it gets loaded with lipids prior to trafficking throughout the body (Palm et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: More than 95% of the hemolymph lipids in Drosophila co-fractionate with Lpp.
source: Lpp is the main hemolymph lipid carrier, since more than 95% of the hemolymph lipids in Drosophila co-fractionate with Lpp (Palm et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: Fat body TAG levels in AKHR1;bmm1 double mutants that harbored Spiroplasma were significantly lower after 12 days than flies with the same genotype that did not harbor Spiroplasma.
source: We found that fat body TAG levels in AKHR1;bmm1 double mutants that harbored Spiroplasma were still significantly lower after 12 days than flies with the same genotype that did not harbor Spiroplasma (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Spiroplasma lipid acquisition most likely occurs in the hemolymph before the point of lipid entry into the fat body stores.
source: While we cannot rule out other, as of yet uncharacterized, lipid mobilization pathways that could theoretically be activated by Spiroplasma, these results are still a strong indication that Spiroplasma lipid acquisition most likely occurs in the hemolymph before the point of lipid entry into the fat body stores.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TAG is depleted even in mutants that cannot mobilize lipids from fat body.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Lpp in the fat body resulted in a decrease in circulating lipoprotein particles and a blockage of lipid export from the gut of Drosophila larvae.
source: A recent study has shown that RNAi-mediated knockdown of Lpp in the fat body resulted in a decrease in circulating lipoprotein particles and a blockage of lipid export from the gut of Drosophila larvae (Palm et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Lpp does not significantly decrease the overall levels of protein in the adult hemolymph.
source: We established that RNAi-mediated knockdown of Lpp does not significantly decrease the overall levels of protein in the adult hemolymph (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) but does decrease adult hemolymph-lipids, as shown by quantification of hemolymph DAG and sterol (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Lpp does decrease adult hemolymph-lipids, as shown by quantification of hemolymph DAG and sterol.
source: We established that RNAi-mediated knockdown of Lpp does not significantly decrease the overall levels of protein in the adult hemolymph (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) but does decrease adult hemolymph-lipids, as shown by quantification of hemolymph DAG and sterol (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 8A and 8B.

claim: Under conditions of Lpp knockdown, Spiroplasma proliferation was severely inhibited resulting in lower Spiroplasma titers in flies after 14, 21, and 28 days of aging.
source: We found that under conditions of Lpp knockdown, Spiroplasma proliferation was severely inhibited resulting in lower Spiroplasma titers in flies after 14, 21, and 28 days of aging (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Lpp strongly diminished Spiroplasma-induced old age mortality.
source: Another striking effect of the RNAi-mediated knockdown of Lpp was strongly diminished Spiroplasma-induced old age mortality (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Spiroplasmas are not known to have the capacity to utilize proteins as nutrient sources.
source: It is noteworthy that Spiroplasmas are not known to have the capacity to utilize proteins as nutrient sources (Chang and Chen, 1983), supporting the claim that lipids carried by Lpp (and not the Lpp protein itself) are the factors required for the proliferation of Spiroplasma.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: Lipids carried by Lpp (and not the Lpp protein itself) are the factors required for the proliferation of Spiroplasma.
source: It is noteworthy that Spiroplasmas are not known to have the capacity to utilize proteins as nutrient sources (Chang and Chen, 1983), supporting the claim that lipids carried by Lpp (and not the Lpp protein itself) are the factors required for the proliferation of Spiroplasma.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Lpp knockdown reduces lipids and inhibits Spiroplasma proliferation, combined with knowledge that Spiroplasma cannot use proteins.

claim: Natural selection is expected to favor vertically transmitted endosymbionts with adaptations that minimize fitness costs to their hosts.
source: Natural selection is expected to favor vertically transmitted endosymbionts with adaptations that minimize fitness costs to their hosts (Werren and O'Neill, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous theoretical work.

claim: Spiroplasma's dependence on hemolymph-lipid availability for proliferation could be of adaptive significance, since it would enable Spiroplasma to limit its proliferation in the face of host nutrient deprivation.
source: We hypothesize that Spiroplasma's dependence on hemolymph-lipid availability for proliferation could be of adaptive significance, since it would enable Spiroplasma to limit its proliferation in the face of host nutrient deprivation, and therefore avoid the costly depletion of its host's energy and other vital metabolites.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: Spiroplasma infection status did not affect the total number of eggs laid over a 14-day period on nutrient rich media.
source: On nutrient rich media, we found that despite increasing early egg production Spiroplasma infection status did not affect the total number of eggs laid over a 14-day period.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on egg production.

claim: Spiroplasma increased by twofold the number of eggs laid by virgin flies over a 14-day period under rich nutritive conditions.
source: Under rich nutritive conditions, we observed that Spiroplasma increased by twofold the number of eggs laid by virgin flies over a 14-day period.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Flies aged for 28 days experience a decline in DAG concentration.
source: It is notable that flies aged for 28 days also experience a decline in DAG concentration, which is likely to explain the declining Spiroplasma proliferation rate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Spiroplasma proliferation over the life of flies results in elevated Spiroplasma titers that ultimately deplete host hemolymph lipid and constrain further proliferation.
source: We suspect that Spiroplasma proliferation over the life of flies results in elevated Spiroplasma titers that ultimately deplete host hemolymph lipid and constrain further proliferation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: Spiroplasma synthesize cardiolipin, most likely using DAG acquired from host lipoproteins.
source: We noted that Spiroplasma-infected flies had higher levels of cardiolipin, suggesting that Spiroplasma synthesize cardiolipin, most likely using DAG acquired from host lipoproteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cardiolipin is present only in Spiroplasma-infected flies and has acyl chains matching depleted DAG species.

claim: The utilization of DAG as a precursor for cardiolipin synthesis is supported by the annotation of the Spiroplasma genome.
source: The utilization of DAG as a precursor for cardiolipin synthesis is supported by the annotation of the Spiroplasma genome (unpublished data), which enabled the identification of a biosynthetic pathway similar to that described in Mycoplasma synoviae and Mycoplasma hyopneumoniae for the synthesis of cardiolipin from acylglycerols through DAG-3-phosphate and cytidine diphosphate-DAG (Arraes et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis and citation to previous studies on related bacteria.

claim: Cardiolipin produced by Spiroplasma could be involved in its pathological effects in old flies.
source: A number of studies have demonstrated links between cardiolipin and cell death (Gonzalvez and Gottlieb, 2007), which raise the possibility that cardiolipin produced by Spiroplasma could be involved in its pathological effects in old flies.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on cited literature and experimental observations.

claim: Sterols have been shown to be required for proliferation of all species of Spiroplasma.
source: Of the other lipid classes contained in lipoproteins, sterols are of particular interest as they have been shown to be required for proliferation of all species of Spiroplasma, and to be highly abundant in the Spiroplasma plasma membrane (Freeman et al., 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: The requirement for sterol is unique to mollicutes amongst bacteria.
source: Amongst bacteria, this requirement for sterol is unique to mollicutes (Dahl, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: Insects are auxotrophic for sterols.
source: Since insects are auxotrophic for sterols (Canavoso et al., 2001), their concentrations are determined by dietary uptake.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: Proliferation and localization of the obligate Sitophilus primary endosymbiont (SPE) is controlled by the expression of a specific antimicrobial peptide from its host, Sitophilus weevils.
source: For example, proliferation and localization of the obligate Sitophilus primary endosymbiont (SPE) is controlled by the expression of a specific antimicrobial peptide from its host, Sitophilus weevils (Login et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: In aphids, studies suggest the activation of the host lysosomal system is involved in controlling titers of the obligate intracellular endosymbiont, Buchnera.
source: In aphids, studies suggest the activation of the host lysosomal system is involved in controlling titers of the obligate intracellular endosymbiont, Buchnera (Nishikori et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: Endosymbiotic Spiroplasma has been implicated in protecting diverse hosts from various eukaryotic parasites including parasitoid wasps, parasitic nematodes, and fungi.
source: Endosymbiotic Spiroplasma has been implicated in a number of cases, including protecting diverse hosts from various eukaryotic parasites including parasitoid wasps, parasitic nematodes, and fungi (Jaenike et al., 2010; Xie et al., 2010; Łukasik et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Spiroplasma-mediated protection could be linked to lipid utilization.
source: We speculate that Spiroplasma-mediated protection could be linked to lipid utilization.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: Many parasitoid wasps are unable to synthesize fatty acids and their development requires the acquisition of host lipids.
source: Indeed, many parasitoid wasps are unable to synthesize fatty acids and their development requires the acquisition of host lipids (Visser et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: Sequestration of lipid by Spiroplasma might limit availability to any parasites or pathogens that occupy the same niche.
source: Thus, sequestration of lipid by Spiroplasma might limit availability to any parasites or pathogens that occupy the same niche.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observation that Spiroplasma depletes lipids.

claim: A variety of other microorganisms known to proliferate in Drosophila hemolymph and to cause pathogenesis such as Erwinia carotovora strain 15, Listeria monocytogenes, Candida albicans, and Enterococcus fecalis do not appear to have attenuated virulence when hemolymph lipids are depleted.
source: It is noteworthy that a variety of other microorganisms known to proliferate in Drosophila hemolymph and to cause pathogenesis such as Erwinia carotovora strain 15, Listeria monocytogenes, Candida albicans, and Enterococcus fecalis do not appear to have attenuated virulence when hemolymph lipids are depleted (unpublished data).
evidence: This is based on unpublished experimental data.

claim: Increased reliance on host provision of lipids is part of a suite of adaptations that facilitate the evolution of chronic, low-virulence infection strategies.
source: It is interesting to speculate that increased reliance on host provision of lipids is part of a suite of adaptations that facilitate the evolution of chronic, low-virulence infection strategies.

claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Chlamydia trachomatis have been shown to be heavily dependent on lipids acquired from their hosts.
source: It is notable that a number of pathogens that have the capacity to form chronic infections in humans including Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Chlamydia trachomatis have been shown to be heavily dependent on lipids acquired from their hosts (Ehrt and Schnappinger, 2007; Robertson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.
